retrieval_text: A 3-year-old boy, the only child of non-consanguineous parents, exhibited widespread warty eruptions covering the body, including the genital area, but excluding the scalp, face, palms, and soles. The skin changes began at 3 weeks of age, initially appearing symmetrically on the anterior thighs, then spreading to the axillae, and over approximately 6 months, progressed to the current widespread distribution. There was no history of blisters or generalized redness at or after birth. The condition showed improvement during summer and worsened in winter. The child was otherwise in good health with no developmental delays or visual or hearing difficulties. There was no significant family history. Physical examination revealed multiple, bilaterally symmetrical, verrucous plaques following the lines of Blaschko, extensively involving the trunk and extremities. The plaques were oriented transversely on the trunk and longitudinally on the limbs. Hair, nails, and oral cavity appeared normal. Systemic examination showed no abnormalities.

A 25-year-old male of Hispanic and Caucasian descent with no significant past medical history arrived at our emergency department from another facility due to sudden paralysis beginning in both lower limbs. He mentioned having received an intraarticular corticosteroid injection in his right knee less than 24 hours before his symptoms began. He also consumed a high carbohydrate meal within five hours before the onset of symptoms. The weakness in his lower limbs spread to his trunk and both upper limbs. By the time of our evaluation, the patient had no symptoms following intravenous correction of low potassium levels at the other facility. At that facility, his vital signs were normal. Physical examination revealed paralysis in his limbs, but his sensation remained intact.

A female child, aged 1 year and 4 months, was admitted for evaluation of delayed psychomotor development and to undergo surgery for exotropia. She was delivered at full term (40 weeks gestation) via cesarean section following an uneventful pregnancy. She is the first child of healthy, unrelated parents, with no notable family medical history. Upon admission, she exhibited a distinctive high-pitched cry and had a smaller than average head size (microcephaly). Motor function delays were observed, including delayed crawling. She could sit without support but was unable to stand, indicating developmental delays compared to typical milestones for her age. Neurologic examination revealed hypotonia in the left leg, while tendon reflexes and cranial nerve function were normal. At 6 months of age, an echocardiogram identified a ventricular septal defect.

A 14-year-old female presented with a two-month history of itchy skin lesions located on the upper and lower extremities, thighs, and pubic area. Her system review did not reveal any other complaints or associated symptoms. Physical examination showed well-demarcated annular brownish plaques, measuring between 5cm and 7cm. The borders of these plaques were scaly and elevated, with a few pustules observed on the upper and lower extremities, thighs, and pubic area. Some lesions exhibited central clearing. There were no abnormalities noted in the hair, nails, mucosal, or genital areas. The patient was treated with terbinafine 250 mg tablets and topical miconazole cream applied twice daily for two weeks. Upon follow-up after two weeks, additional lesions were observed on the lower extremity and inner thigh, despite adherence to the prescribed treatment.

A 13-year-old girl presented with difficulty breathing, subcutaneous nodules, and joint pain over the past three months. The joint pain, which developed gradually, affected her knees, ankles, elbows, wrists, and fingers bilaterally, more on the right side, and worsened over time, impacting her daily activities. The pain was severe at night and early morning, causing her to miss school. Initially, she responded to Ibuprofen, but later it became ineffective. The pain was accompanied by swelling and redness around the joints. Two months after the onset of joint pain, her mother noticed small, round, non-tender, skin-colored subcutaneous nodules on her elbows and arms. Subsequently, the patient began experiencing chest pain and difficulty breathing with exertion, which worsened when lying down. She had a history of an upper respiratory tract infection and high fever (39-40ºC) two weeks before the joint pain, which lasted a week and improved with antipyretics. She visited multiple healthcare facilities before being referred to our hospital. Over the last three months, she experienced joint pain, subcutaneous nodules, and exertional dyspnea. She was admitted for management and further investigation. There was no recent history of palpitations, rash, coughing up blood, mood swings, or abnormal movements. On physical examination, she appeared in pain, with a temperature of 37ºC. Her respiratory rate was 28/min, heart rate was 129/min, and blood pressure was 126/70 mmHg. She measured 153 cm in height, weighed 81 kg, and had a BMI of 35. Cardiovascular examination revealed a grade 3 holosystolic murmur with the highest intensity at the apex. She exhibited an antalgic gait and had subcutaneous nodules on the extensor surface of the right elbow and interphalangeal joints, with no signs of arthritis.

An 83-year-old Caucasian male, farmer, presented with sudden onset pain and redness in his right eye. He had no history of ocular trauma or previous ocular surgery, and no relevant family history or ophthalmological conditions. He was not on any topical or systemic medication. The patient had been known to the clinic for 3 months with a hypermature cataract in the right eye and a mature cataract in the left eye. He was scheduled for cataract extraction in the left eye first, followed by the right eye. During the preoperative consultation for the left eye cataract surgery, he reported acute ocular pain and photophobia in the right eye that began a few days prior. Clinical examination showed visual acuity of light perception in the right eye and counting fingers in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was 50 mmHg in the right eye and 13 mmHg in the left eye.

A two-year-old boy was referred to our department due to a distal diaphyseal fracture of the left femur. He is the first child of non-consanguineous parents. At birth, his weight, length, and occipital-frontal circumference were around the 25th percentile. His mother, a 26-year-old primagravida, had no history of spontaneous abortions, stillbirths, or neonatal mortalities and was married to a 27-year-old unrelated man. At birth, the child had plagiocephaly and was treated with a cranial band (Care band), which he wore for 23 hours per day until he was one year old. No skull radiographs were taken at that time. His development included motor delay, but other developmental skills were within the normal range. There was no history of visual, auditory, or other neurological symptoms, nor was there any history of anorexia, weight loss, or muscular hypotonia. Examination at the age of two years showed a pleasant boy with mild and unnoticeable facial features, including frontal bossing and slight facial asymmetry with incomplete auricular folding. There were no signs of leontiasis ossea, Cushingoid facies, macrocephaly, retarded growth, or muscular hypotonia. Neurological, ophthalmological, and auditory evaluations were normal, with no history of seizures or non-motor developmental delay.

The patient is a 7-year-old male. Clinical findings include atresia of the choanae, which was surgically treated, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and micropenis, managed with luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone analogue therapy, and a bicuspid aortic valve. There is asymmetry of the buccal rhyme when crying and smiling due to hypoplasia of the left mouth corner depressor. The patient exhibits motor impediment and mild craniofacial dysmorphisms, such as slightly low implanted pinnae, a prominent nasal root, hypoplastic nasal wings, mid-facial hypoplasia, and a high and narrow palate. Corrective lenses are used for myopia. An ENT evaluation documented very slight bilateral conductive hearing loss. Re-evaluation of CT radiograms taken at birth indicated 'inner ear dysplasia'.

A 10-year-old male patient presented with irregularly positioned front teeth. The patient had a history of bilateral congenital cataracts, which were surgically treated at 6 months of age, and he wore corrective spectacles. His medical history was otherwise unremarkable, and there was no significant family history. Extraoral examination showed mild facial dysmorphism, including a long narrow face, mandibular prognathism, a large narrow nose with a high narrow nasal bridge, and large protruding anteverted ears. The patient exhibited no signs of intellectual impairment, performed well in school, and responded appropriately to instructions. Intraoral examination revealed multiple dental anomalies: incisors with conical or screwdriver shapes and notched incised edges, prominent Talon's cusps on the upper lateral incisors, and molars with central supernumerary cusps and a globular appearance. Generalized spacing was observed, with a predominantly permanent dentition except for unerupted permanent canines. Numerous carious lesions were present in the permanent molars. A blood serological investigation was conducted.

A 70-year-old woman visited the outpatient breast clinic due to changes in the skin of her left breast. She observed skin discoloration 6 months prior, which progressively increased, prompting her to seek medical attention. Her medical history includes hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, and osteoporosis, with no previous breast health issues or surgeries. She reported no associated symptoms such as pain, new masses, nipple discharge/retraction, or lymphadenopathy. During the physical examination, her vital signs were within normal limits, and she appeared to be in no distress. The breast examination revealed a single 3 × 3 cm pink, non-tender, raised lesion on the left breast at the 12:00 position. The patient agreed to a treatment procedure and tolerated it well without any complications.

A 41-year-old Japanese woman came to the clinic with a 4-month history of pain in both groins and the right buttock, with the right hip being more painful than the left. She had no history of trauma, alcohol abuse, or steroid use. Her medical history included iron-deficiency anemia diagnosed 2 years prior, for which she had been taking iron supplements. She had no previous fractures, including fragility fractures. Her height was 155 cm, her weight was 42 kg, and her body mass index was 18.7 kg/m2. She could walk for about 10 minutes without assistance, though at a slow pace. Limitations in passive motion of both hip joints were noted: flexion was 100°, internal rotation was 5°, external rotation was 15°, and abduction was 20° on both sides. She could perform a straight-leg raise of the right limb with significant pain. The neurovascular status of both lower extremities was normal. According to the Japanese Orthopaedic Association scoring system for hip-joint function, her right hip scored 46 points and her left hip scored 56 points out of a possible 100 points, with the score comprising 40 points for pain, 20 for range of motion, 20 for the ability to walk, and 20 for activities of daily living.

A 56-year-old Japanese man presented with a 3-month history of asymptomatic brown follicular hyperkeratotic plaque/papules spread across the body, with significant hair loss on the scalp. Some papules exhibited a comedo-like appearance and/or signs of infection. Additionally, there was a slight reduction in pubic and axillary hair growth. The patient had been on dialysis for 3 years due to chronic renal failure. There was no family history of similar conditions, no use of medications related to the symptoms, and no exposure to dioxins. The patient did not have COVID-19 and had not

retrieval_text: A 26-year-old female reported experiencing vision loss and metamorphopsia in her left eye over the past five days. Her refractive error was measured at -7.25 D in both eyes. The best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/20 (6/6 in Snellen visual acuity of 6 meters) in the right eye and 20/40 (6/12 in Snellen visual acuity of 6 meters) in the left eye. Examination of the anterior chamber and vitreous cavity showed no signs of inflammation. Fundoscopy of the left eye revealed sporadic, small, round, yellow-white spots confined to the posterior pole, with no evidence of hemorrhage.

A 5-month-old girl, born full-term via vaginal delivery, presented with a history of fever followed by seizure and subsequent unilateral body weakness. There was no prior history of seizures, and her motor and language development were appropriate for her age. According to her parents, she was in her usual state of health and behaving normally before developing a fever. A few hours after the onset of fever, she experienced a seizure. She was brought to Gandhi Memorial Hospital (GMH), Rewa, while actively seizing and was administered intravenous midazolam, phenytoin, valproate, and levetiracetam. Following the seizure, she exhibited weakness on the left side of her body. The seizure lasted approximately 10–15 hours in total. By the third day of hospitalization, her mental status had improved, but she still showed left-sided hemiparesis and was not speaking spontaneously. Over the next four days, her condition began to improve with continued antiepileptic treatment.

A woman in her early twenties with a lifelong history of alopecia presented with 2–3 months of intermittent, dull, throbbing, and localized tenderness in one of the alopecic patches. The affected area, located on the right parietal-occipital scalp, had been stable in size and appearance since birth. Additionally, three other round patches of alopecia, also present since birth, remained asymptomatic. Clinical examination of the scalp revealed an atrophic white patch of alopecia. Surrounding the lesion, there was ill-defined bogginess extending to the central and posterior occipital scalp.

An 11-year-old male presented to a tertiary care hospital with a history of progressively increasing seizure frequency since infancy. The patient exhibited delayed developmental milestones and right-sided hemiparesis. Seizures were predominantly right-sided, complex partial in nature, and resistant to medical treatment over the past ten years. The child was born at term through a normal vaginal delivery to parents who are not related by blood. There is no family history of neurological conditions.

A 7-year-old boy presented with behavioral issues since infancy. His early developmental history indicated he was the first child, born from an unplanned pregnancy. At 36 weeks of gestation, the mother experienced oligohydramnios, and possible congenital cardiac defects were noted in the fetus. The child was delivered preterm at 36 weeks via emergency cesarean section due to fetal bradycardia. His birth weight was 1.7 kg, he had a delayed cry, and was cyanosed at birth. Cardiac evaluation at birth identified cardiac anomalies including patent ductus arteriosus, ventricular septal defect, tricuspid regurgitation, and a left atrium to right atrium shunt. He was started on digitoxin. As he grew, he exhibited global developmental delay and was diagnosed with bilateral profound sensorineural hearing loss at 6 months of age. Over time, he continued to show delayed milestones and developed behaviors such as poor eye contact, poor social and communication skills, repetitive head rocking, hand flapping movements, and a preference for fixed routines. From the age of 3, he displayed symptoms of attention deficit hyperkinetic disorder (ADHD), including an inability to sit still for more than 2-3 minutes and difficulty engaging in activities. His insistence on routine and hyperactivity increased over the years, leading to aggressive behaviors such as hitting and biting his mother, which resulted in significant distress and a psychiatry consultation with subsequent admission to a child psychiatry inpatient unit. There was no history of head injury, seizures, frequent diarrhea and vomiting, birthmarks, or failure to thrive. Physical examination revealed a small head circumference (49 cm) and bilateral flat feet. Mental status examination showed a lack of eye contact, hyperactivity, irritable mood, frequent side-to-side head movements, and hand flapping. His intelligence quotient was evaluated to be 25.

A 37-year-old Japanese man underwent imaging, which revealed a 10 mm cystic lesion with a mural nodule near the anterior horn of the right lateral ventricle. Despite the absence of neurological symptoms, the patient was monitored over a period of 10 years. During this time, the lesion increased in size from 10 mm to 18 mm, and the patient experienced worsening headaches.

A 32-year-old male reported experiencing chest pain and shortness of breath for the past 2 months. He did not have a cough, expectoration, or hemoptysis, and there was no swelling or lump in any limbs. There was no history of abdominal pain or weight loss, and the patient did not have a history of tobacco smoking or other addictions. On physical examination, his pulse rate was 92 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 20 per minute, blood pressure was 116/78 mmHg, and oxygen saturation was 95%. Chest examination indicated a dull note on percussion and absent breath sounds in the entire right hemithorax, except for the right infraclavicular area where breath sounds were normal. A chest radiograph revealed a large, nonhomogeneous opacity in the right hemithorax, denser in the middle and lower lung zones, with mild displacement of the mediastinum toward the left. Ultrasonography (USG) identified a large, heterogeneous, hypoechoic mass lesion in the right hemithorax with intratumoral vessels visible on Doppler examination. USG of the abdomen showed no evidence of abdominal mass or metastasis.

A 12-year-old female patient was referred to our retina service due to a decrease in visual acuity in her right eye. She had a history of strabismus, hyperopia, and amblyopia in the right eye. Her mother had undergone surgery for skin cancer and maxillary cysts. The patient had multiple odontogenic cysts and scoliosis and had been previously evaluated in Neuropediatrics for macrocephaly. Her intellectual capacity was normal. Clinical examination showed visual acuity of 20/80 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Anterior segment evaluation showed no abnormalities, and intraocular pressure was normal in both eyes. Fundus examination revealed an elevated lesion in the temporal region of the macula, white-greyish in color, with associated vascular distortion, causing significant traction in the macular area.
